reason: The heart muscle fits the chamber outline and should provide the squeezing force needed for the first goal.
expectation: The muscle will surround the chambers so they can squeeze.

effect: The chambers can squeeze, but fluid moves toward both openings, so they need a way to prevent backward flow.
reaction: The arrows make the remaining problem clear.
reason: The valve picture shows cusps closing against reverse flow.
expectation: The valves should direct blood forward during a squeeze.

effect: The valves direct flow forward during squeezing and allow the chambers to refill; repeated squeezes still need coordination.
reaction: The squeeze and refill panels make the valves’ role clear.
reason: The pacemaker cells are shown producing a spreading electrical wave, suggesting they coordinate repeated heartbeats.
expectation: The pacemaker cells will help the heart squeeze repeatedly.

effect: The pacemaker completes the beating pump; the remaining goal needs blood and a returning vessel route.
reaction: The distinction between starting the beat and nerves adjusting it was interesting.
reason: Hemoglobin binds oxygen, and the flexible envelopes provide the structure for red blood cells.
expectation: This should make oxygen-carrying red blood cells.

effect: The red blood cells can carry oxygen and make ATP from sugar without mitochondria. Plasma is still needed to make blood.
reaction: The contrast with the muscle cells was interesting.
reason: Plasma is the fluid component that can carry the red blood cells.

effect: The blood is assembled, including red cells in plasma; the pump and returning vessel route still need to be connected.
reaction: The inset clarifies that blood includes more than red cells and plasma.
reason: The capillary networks can connect the outgoing arteries with the returning veins.
expectation: The vessels should form a connected route for blood to travel out and return.

effect: The arteries, capillaries and veins now form a circuit with slots for the pump and transport medium.
reaction: The marked slots make the remaining assembly clear.
reason: The beating heart fits the circuit's pump slot.
expectation: The heart will be fitted into the vessel circuit as its pump.

effect: The beating heart is connected to the outgoing and returning vessels; the transport medium slot still needs blood.
reaction: The circuit is taking shape clearly.
reason: Oxygen-carrying blood fits the circuit's transport medium slot.
expectation: The blood will be fitted into the pumped vessel circuit.

effect: The blood completed the circuit, showing how oxygen and nutrients can reach tissue while blood returns to the heart.
reaction: The tissue-exchange inset helped connect the assembled circuit to cellular work.

mostWorthwhile.text: Adding the blood was most worthwhile because the completed circuit showed both delivery to tissues and the return route.

leastWorthwhile.text: Fitting the heart and blood into named slots was clear but predictable; those steps offered little uncertainty once the circuit was built.

surprise.text: I was interested that red blood cells make ATP from sugar despite having no mitochondria, unlike the muscle cells described earlier.

arbitrary.text: None of the actions felt particularly arbitrary; the pictures and goals gave each part a clear role.

continue.text: I would continue for another chapter to see how the circuit connects with other body systems, although the final slot-filling steps were predictable.
